q: Iron has atomic number 26. Its ground-state electronic configuration is:
x: After argon (18 electrons), the 4s orbital takes 2 and the 3d subshell takes the remaining 6. Iron has no special half-filled or filled d arrangement, so it is 3d⁶ 4s².

q: How many unpaired electrons does a gaseous Co²⁺ ion have (Co, Z = 27)?
x: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; losing the two 4s electrons gives Co²⁺ = 3d⁷. Five electrons go singly into the five 3d orbitals and two more pair up, leaving 3 unpaired. Seven is the total d count, not the unpaired count.

q: A ground-state nickel atom (Ni, Z = 28) has how many unpaired electrons?
x: Ni is [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². The 4s pair is full; in 3d⁸ three orbitals are paired and two hold single electrons, giving 2 unpaired.

q: Titanium has atomic number 22. The electronic configuration of a gaseous Ti²⁺ ion is:
x: Ti is [Ar] 3d² 4s². On ionisation the 4s electrons are lost first, so Ti²⁺ is [Ar] 3d². Keeping 4s² and removing the 3d electrons is the common mistake.

q: Which pair of gaseous ions has the same number of unpaired electrons?
x: Ti³⁺ is 3d¹ and Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, and each has one unpaired electron. V³⁺ has 2, Cr³⁺ has 3, Mn²⁺ has 5 and Ni²⁺ has 2.

q: A first-row transition metal ion has a spin-only magnetic moment of 3.87 BM. Using μ = √(n(n + 2)), the number of unpaired electrons, n, is:
x: n = 3 gives √(3 × 5) = √15 ≈ 3.87 BM. n = 2 gives √8 ≈ 2.83 BM and n = 4 gives √24 ≈ 4.90 BM.
Sc³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁰ with no unpaired electrons, so it is diamagnetic. Ti³⁺ (3d¹), V³⁺ (3d²) and Cr³⁺ (3d³) all have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic.

q: Many compounds of transition elements are attracted into a magnetic field (they are paramagnetic). This is due to:
o: Paired electrons in their p orbitals
Unpaired electrons in their d orbitals
x: Paramagnetism comes from unpaired electrons, and transition metal ions often have partly filled d subshells with unpaired electrons. Paired electrons do not cause attraction into a field.

q: In potassium permanganate, KMnO₄, manganese (Mn: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²) is in the +7 state. How many 3d electrons does manganese have in this state?
x: Mn has 7 electrons beyond argon (3d⁵ 4s²). In the +7 state all seven are used, leaving 3d⁰. Five is the number in the neutral atom.

q: In the complex ion [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, each cyanide ligand carries a charge of −1. The d-electron configuration of iron (Z = 26) in this ion is:
x: Fe + 6(−1) = −4 gives Fe = +2, and Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶. Taking iron as +3 would wrongly give 3d⁵.

q: Which two elements of the first transition series have only one electron in the 4s orbital of their ground-state atoms?
x: Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because a half-filled or completely filled 3d subshell gives extra stability. The other elements listed have 4s².

q: Chromium's ground-state atom is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². The reason is that:
o: The 4s orbital can hold only one electron in chromium
A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell has extra stability
A completely filled 3d subshell is formed
x: Moving one 4s electron into 3d gives a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, which is especially stable. The 4s orbital can still hold two electrons, and 3d⁵ is half-filled, not full.

q: A first-row transition element has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d³ 4s². The element is:
x: 18 + 3 + 2 = 23 electrons, so Z = 23, vanadium. Chromium has 24 electrons and is 3d⁵ 4s¹.

q: Which gaseous ion has exactly four electrons in its 3d subshell?
x: Mn is 3d⁵ 4s²; removing the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron gives Mn³⁺ = 3d⁴. Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ are 3d⁵, and Cr³⁺ is 3d³.

q: What is the total number of electrons in a gaseous Fe³⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26)?
x: A neutral Fe atom has 26 electrons; losing 3 leaves 23. Adding 3 to get 29 is the sign mistake, and 24 is the count for Fe²⁺.

q: Moving across the first transition series, the first ground-state atom to have a completely filled 3d subshell is:
x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, so the 3d subshell becomes full one element before zinc (3d¹⁰ 4s²). Nickel is still 3d⁸ and cobalt 3d⁷.

q: Iron(III) compounds are often more stable than iron(II) compounds. In terms of electronic structure, this is because:
o: Fe³⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
Fe³⁺ keeps both of its 4s electrons
x: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ while Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵, a half-filled subshell with extra stability. Fe²⁺ actually has 4 unpaired electrons, and both 4s electrons are lost in Fe³⁺.

q: d-block elements are called transition elements mainly because they:
o: All have completely filled d subshells in their atoms
Change into other elements by radioactive decay
Have their last electron entering an s orbital
Lie between the s-block and p-block, with properties intermediate between them
x: They sit between the reactive s-block metals and the p-block elements, and their properties show a transition between the two. Their last electron enters a d orbital, and most have partly filled d subshells.
